issues.explanation: The profile is for a 61-year-old bus driver who witnessed trauma. 'Bicycle' as a trigger is not impossible, but in combination with the rest of the profile it points toward a very specific accident scenario that is not supported elsewhere in the report. The other items emphasize guilt, sensory reliving, and contamination/interpersonal avoidance, creating a mixed picture that is hard to unify around a single witnessed-trauma account.

issues.item: Negative Appraisals: Contamination: I feel dirty or contaminated because of what happened
issues.explanation: Feeling 'dirty or contaminated' is much more characteristic of sexual or contact-based interpersonal trauma than of witnessed trauma. For a witnessed-trauma formulation, this appraisal is difficult to reconcile unless there was direct bodily involvement, which is not reflected elsewhere.

Avoiding sex is hard to explain from the rest of this profile. The selected memory and appraisal items center on reliving and guilt about inaction, but do not support a coherent mechanism for sexual avoidance in a witnessed-trauma case.

vignette:
Ines, a 61-year-old bus driver with thirty years of impeccable service, arrived at her first session accompanied by her husband, though he waited in the reception area. She described her life as having split into two distinct periods: before the accident, and after. The accident itself happened four months ago, on a bright Tuesday morning. A small sedan, two cars ahead of her bus, swerved to avoid a piece of debris and lost control, spinning directly into the path of an oncoming truck. Ines had slammed on the brakes, the bus lurching to a halt just feet from the collision. She was trapped in her elevated driver’s seat, a helpless observer to the screech of tires, the crush of metal, and then a profound, ringing silence. She saw blood on the shattered windshield of the car, a sight that is now seared into her mind.

In the weeks that followed, the event refused to remain in the past. The memory would ambush her without warning, and when it came, it was not a recollection but a full-sensory reliving. She would be standing in her kitchen and suddenly smell the acrid smoke from the sedan’s engine and feel the phantom vibration of her own bus’s brakes locking up. The memory felt so intensely present that she would sometimes reach out to brace herself against a non-existent dashboard. Because the accident felt as though it was perpetually on the verge of reoccurring, the normal sounds of traffic became a constant source of threat, each squeal of brakes or distant siren a potential prelude to disaster. This vivid re-experiencing relentlessly fed her belief that she had failed in some fundamental way. Each time the scene played out in her mind, she was struck by her own immobility, her inability to have done anything more than watch. The thought became a conviction: she should have been able to protect them, and her failure was unforgivable.

This crushing sense of guilt began to shape her daily existence. The more she dwelled on her perceived inaction, the more frequently the memories would surface, as if her mind were forcing her to re-examine the scene for further proof of her culpability. This constant self-blame also made her hyper-aware of potential dangers on the road. Driving her route, once a source of quiet pride, became an exercise in dread. Any car that braked suddenly or the distant wail of a siren would trigger a jolt of panic. These moments didn't just frighten her; they immediately confirmed her deepest fears about herself. A minor fender-bender on the opposite side of the highway became a personal indictment: 'See? It can happen anywhere, and I am powerless to stop it.' The sight of crumpled metal, no matter how insignificant, was a direct reminder of her failure.

To manage the overwhelming guilt and the terrifyingly real memories, Ines developed a set of rigid, private behaviours. Before starting her bus each morning, she now performs a silent ritual, reciting the names of her children and grandchildren seven times to ensure their safety. She believes this frantic mental act is the only thing preventing another tragedy. This daily ritual, intended to ward off danger, had the paradoxical effect of putting her on high alert for it; having spent the morning focused on preventing a catastrophe, she would then spend her entire shift scanning the road for the first sign of one. The horror of the memory also led her to withdraw from all physical contact. The simple act of her husband placing a hand on her shoulder feels like an unbearable intrusion, a sensory overload that threatens to pull her back to the accident scene. This avoidance has carved a painful distance between them, deepening her sense that her life is no longer worth living.

These strategies have only tightened the trap. The mental rituals, designed to provide control, serve as a constant reminder of the very event she is trying to escape, ensuring the memory remains fresh and accessible. Her avoidance of touch has left her profoundly isolated, reinforcing her belief that she is broken beyond repair. This isolation, in turn, makes it harder to dismiss the intrusive thoughts of her failure. At times, the raw emotion of the trauma—a wave of pure, image-less dread and grief—will wash over her, a feeling she has come to associate with her own worthlessness.

She has come to therapy because the rituals are no longer enough to keep the terror at bay, and the chasm between her and her husband has grown too wide to ignore. She feels exhausted by the constant vigilance, by the mental loops of guilt and fear. Her greatest fear, she stated quietly, is not that another accident will happen, but that she is right about herself—that she is a person who failed when it mattered most, and that she will never be able to forgive herself.

The causal relationship is absent because the vignette does not describe how Ines's safety behaviours (rituals, avoidance) make her more sensitive or hypervigilant to external triggers.

vignette_attempts.feedback:
REQUIRED EDGES MISSING:
- Memory → Triggers: The causal relationship is absent because the vignette does not describe how the trauma memory makes Ines more hyper-aware of or sensitive to triggering stimuli.
  e.g. "After the memory had surfaced, even the most ordinary things — a kettle whistling, a door slamming — felt like warnings she couldn't afford to ignore."
  e.g. "The intrusive image left her scanning every room she entered, cataloguing exits, tracking faces, unable to switch off."
  e.g. "Because the memory came back so vividly, she began to see threads of it everywhere: in strangers' faces, in certain times of day, in the quality of winter light."
- Maladaptive Strategies → Triggers: The causal relationship is absent because the vignette does not describe how Ines's safety behaviours (rituals, avoidance) make her more sensitive or hypervigilant to external triggers.
  e.g. "Each place she avoided became a reminder in itself — the long way round she walked every morning was its own daily acknowledgement of what had happened."
  e.g. "Her safety behaviours had drawn a map of the event around her: everything she couldn't do, everywhere she couldn't go, every person she kept at arm's length."
  e.g. "The avoidance had grown in all directions until the city was full of routes she no longer used and things she could no longer say."
